# Why code at all

Exercise 5.1 gave you 25 minutes to read one gene off a database record.
Chapter 20 hands you a table with 27,179 rows in it, and every row is a gene.
The same job on every one of them, no shortcuts. How long?

## The wall

That 25 is the budget the exercise printed, and nobody timed you. The estimates
in this book lean short, as Chapter 3 warned, and doubling one is ordinary. Put
your own number in below if you wrote it down. The round ten thousand keeps the
arithmetic readable, and the real table is nearly three times bigger.

```{python}
minutes = 25 * 10000
print(minutes, "minutes")
print(round(minutes / 60), "hours")
print(round(minutes / 60 / 3), "weeks at three hours a week")
print(round(minutes / 60 / 3 / 52), "years")
```

<!-- nlr-allow: 10000 250000 4167 1389 9360 250 -->

Three hours a week is the budget Chapter 1 asked you for, so those are your
weeks. Twenty-seven years. That's the honest answer to the question at the top
of this page. You don't finish.

Work out where you'd actually stop. Three hours a week for a year is 156 hours,
which is 9,360 minutes. Divide by 25 and you get 374. A year of your evenings,
every evening you promised, and you've read 374 of the 27,179 rows. That's
under two percent.

::: {.check}
Type those four lines into a Colab cell and put your own time in place of the
25. If Exercise 5.1 cost you 40 minutes, the last line comes back 43. Any time
you could plausibly have taken lands in years. Weeks means you dropped a zero
out of the ten thousand.
:::

You've already seen that wall from the other side. The tardigrade paper in
Chapter 9 ran the Chapter 6 question against more than twenty thousand
predicted genes, and nobody did that through a form. Past a few hundred of
anything, the size of the job picks the tool, and you don't get a vote.

That's the speed argument. Everybody makes it for code, it's true, and it's the
weaker half of the case.

This is the one chapter in the book with nothing for you to hand in, so its If
it breaks section sits here, beside the only cell it has, rather than at the
end.

## If it breaks

Both of these come from typing the four lines rather than pasting them, and
both are Python talking rather than the notebook or the website.

::: {.ifbreaks}
::: {.errfix err="NameError: name 'minutes' is not defined"}
Python has never been handed anything called `minutes`. All four lines have to
run in the same runtime, in order. If the `print` lines are sitting in their own
cell, or the runtime disconnected in between, the first line is gone. Run the
line that sets `minutes` again, then the prints.
:::

::: {.errfix err="TypeError: unsupported operand type(s) for /: 'tuple' and 'int'"}
You typed the ten thousand with a comma in it. In Python a comma separates two
values, and it's never part of a number. So `25 * 10,000` is `25 * 10`, which is
250, followed by `000`, which is 0. `minutes` holds that pair, and a pair can't
be divided by 60. Look at what the first line printed: `(250, 0) minutes`,
brackets and all. Take the comma out.
:::
:::

## Six months later

Go and find your Chapter 5 answer sheet. One of the five values on it is an
accession with a version suffix. Now answer something the sheet doesn't say.
On the evening you wrote that suffix down, was it the one the page was showing,
or had you copied it off this book?

If you can answer, it's because you recorded where the number came from as well
as the number. Nothing on the screen asked you to.

A click leaves nothing behind. Your browser keeps a list of pages you visited,
and a list of pages is not a list of decisions. Which menu you opened, which of
the three exon counts you settled on, whether you carried the version suffix
along: none of that is written down anywhere. And it isn't in your memory six
months on.

These are the second and third of the limits Chapter 9 named, taken apart.
Three consequences follow, and they get worse in that order.

You can't repeat it exactly. You'll click slightly differently next time, and
the site will have moved its labels in between, and neither difference
announces itself.

Nobody else can check it. A stranger reading your result has your number and no
route to it, and nothing to disagree with except your word.

And there's no artifact. Ask what Chapter 5 actually produced, as an object. A
few numbers on an answer sheet. Hand that to somebody and you've handed them a
claim.

The third one costs you more than the other two. Chapter 1 promised you'd
finish this book with your code somewhere a stranger can open it. That's what
somebody with no affiliation puts in front of a hiring manager in place of a
reference. An evening of clicking produces nothing openable. It was real work,
and it leaves no evidence that it happened.

::: {.why}
The tardigrade result in Chapter 9 turned on exactly this. Koutsovoulos and
colleagues didn't have to take the first group's judgment on faith. They ran
the work again on their own data and compared, and the estimate moved from
about one-sixth of the genes to at most 1 to 2 percent. Redoing an analysis is
the mechanism biology has for finding out that a published result was about the
sample rather than the animal. It runs on other people being able to repeat
what you did.
:::

## What a script actually is

A [script]{.term def="A list of instructions saved in a file, so a machine can
run the same steps again without you retyping them."} is a list of instructions
saved in a file. The whole definition fits in that sentence, and it's smaller
than the word sounds.

Here's your Chapter 5 job written as one.

``` {.default}
1. Open the NCBI Gene record for BRCA1 in human.
2. Read off the MANE Select transcript accession, version and all.
3. Fetch that transcript.
4. Count its bases.
5. Print the accession and the count on one line.
```

Those five lines are English, and they're already a script in every sense but
the one that matters: no machine can read them. Trade the English for Python
and something else changes as well: the list stops describing what you did and
starts being the thing that does it.

Now the property you're buying, stated narrowly. Given the same input, a script
produces the same output next year, and on a machine belonging to somebody who
has never met you. Nothing more than that is on offer. Your five steps stop
being a memory and become a file, so the question "which transcript did you
use" gets answered by line 2 without anybody having to ask you.

The machine belonging to somebody else is less abstract than it sounds, because
you've already been working on one. Everything you write from here on runs on a
Colab machine that Google starts for you. A link to that notebook is a link
somebody else can open and run against the same data. What travels is the
instructions rather than the answers, which is the difference between showing
your work and reporting it.

::: {.trap}
Read "the same input" slowly. A script that fetches whatever NCBI currently
calls `NM_007294` isn't getting the same input each run, because the record
gets corrected and the number after the dot goes up. Run it in 2028 and it
answers a slightly different question, in the same format, at the same speed,
with no complaint anywhere. Pin the version or save the sequence file beside
the script, and the promise holds.
:::

## For one gene, clicking wins

For one gene, once, the browser beats the script and it isn't close. The next
six chapters are slow, and 25 minutes of clicking sits against a couple of
evenings of finding out what a variable is.

Here's the crossover, and both numbers in it are soft. A lookup costs 25
minutes, which is the exercise budget rather than anything I timed. Say the
first script you write costs you three hours, which is 180 minutes. Divide one
by the other. You get 7.2, so it pays for itself somewhere around the eighth
gene.

Treat 7.2 as the pessimistic figure, because the real crossover sits lower.
Nobody runs an analysis once. You run it, you notice the numbers came off
the wrong transcript, and you run it again. A second run of a script costs a
keypress. A second run of a click-path costs the full 25 minutes, and the
fourth run costs 25 more.

Put your own two numbers on that scale once you have them. The arithmetic
matters less than the shape: one side is paid once, and the other side is paid
every single time.

One more item sits on the clicking side of the ledger, and it's a real one. A
web form checks what you typed and complains on the spot. You met that in
Chapter 6, where pasting the wrong characters gets your sequence refused before
anything runs. A script you wrote yourself checks nothing, runs your mistake at
full speed, and prints an answer. There's a section in Chapter 16 on finding a
wrong answer that never errored, and this is what it's for.

## What the next six chapters buy you

Concretely, and in the order they arrive.

- Chapter 11 turns a sequence into something you can measure: its length, a
  slice of it, how many of its bases are G or C. The off-by-one that Chapter 5
  warned you about gets a long section to itself.
- A loop does one thing to every item in a pile, and the code stays the same
  length whether the pile holds 5 sequences or 27,179. Chapter 12, and it's the
  one that answers the question at the top of this page.
- The genetic code becomes a lookup table in Chapter 13, which is also the
  shape of every gene-symbol mapping you'll ever need.
- By Chapter 14 you write translation once and call it by name, after you've
  written the same four lines twice by hand and felt why.
- Files that real people send you get opened in Chapter 15, including a FASTA
  with a blank line dropped into the middle of it.
- Ten pages on reading error messages sit in Chapter 16. It's the chapter that
  decides whether you're still doing this in six months.

None of those is Python for its own sake. Variables come first, and they start
where you already are: one sequence, and a name to put on it.
